# Shown when a product card is expanded. 2-4 sentences.
# Same key scheme and same style rules as descriptions.tsv — never name the vendor.
# Shape: how it works, what people use it for, then one honest thing to know.

column2: NNMT is the enzyme that breaks down nicotinamide, and fat cells make a lot of it as they expand. Blocking it raises NAD+ inside the cell and pushes fat cells toward burning rather than storing. Most of the interesting work is in cell and animal models, with human data still thin — treat the body-recomposition claims as promising rather than proven.

AMPK is the sensor that tells a cell it's running low on energy, and switching it on triggers the same adaptations as endurance training. It became famous as the original "exercise in a bottle" and is banned in competitive sport for that reason. Injectable only and expensive at effective doses, which is why it stays niche.

This is a modified version of the tail end of growth hormone, the part responsible for fat breakdown. Because the growth-signalling portion is removed, it doesn't raise IGF-1 or affect blood sugar the way full GH does. Human trials were underwhelming at the doses tested, so expect a mild effect rather than a dramatic one.

A pan-AMPK activator, meaning it switches on all the AMPK subunits rather than just one. Research centres on insulin sensitivity, glucose uptake and vascular function in metabolic disease models. Very little human data exists, so this is early-stage.

Mitochondrial uncouplers let energy escape as heat instead of being captured as ATP, so you burn more calories at rest. This is the same mechanism as DNP, but BAM15 has a far wider safety margin because it doesn't affect the cell membrane the same way. Still, it's an uncoupler — the dose-response is steep and overheating is the known risk class.

Blocks the enzyme that keeps pyruvate out of the mitochondria, pushing cells to fully oxidise glucose rather than ferment it to lactate. Researched for metabolic and mitochondrial conditions. Human data is limited and mostly from outside the West.

A potent stimulant that works through noradrenaline release, producing sharp focus and appetite suppression. It was pulled from the US supplement market over cardiovascular safety concerns. Blood pressure response is significant and stacking it with other stimulants is where people get into trouble.

Thyroid hormone drives fat loss but also strains the heart. GC-1 was designed to activate the thyroid receptor mainly in the liver, lowering cholesterol and raising fat oxidation without the same cardiac load. Human trials exist for lipid lowering; it is still not an approved drug anywhere.

The last 15 amino acids of growth hormone, isolated because that fragment carries the fat-burning activity without the growth signalling. In theory you get lipolysis with no effect on IGF-1, blood sugar or tissue growth. In practice human results have been modest, and it's typically run alongside a GH secretagogue rather than alone.

Lipotropics are compounds that help the liver process and export fat — typically methionine, inositol and choline. The injection is used alongside a calorie deficit for fat metabolism and liver support, not as a standalone fat loss tool. Think of it as support for the process rather than the driver of it.

Methionine, inositol and choline with B12. Methionine and choline help the liver package and clear fat; B12 supports the energy pathways involved. Commonly given weekly in weight-management clinics as an adjunct — the evidence for fat loss on its own is weak.
A lipotropic blend with added B12 for the energy side. Used weekly alongside a deficit, usually in combination with a GLP-1 rather than instead of one. Benefits are supportive rather than dramatic.

A higher-strength lipotropic formulation of the same methionine, inositol and choline family. Same role: liver fat processing and energy support alongside a calorie deficit. Dose strength varies by vendor, so check the label rather than assuming it matches a standard Lipo-C.

Pairs a strong central appetite suppressant with an NNMT inhibitor that works on the fat cell itself, in a strip that dissolves under the tongue. The format avoids injections and first-pass metabolism. Tesofensine is the active half here and carries a real stimulant load — blood pressure and sleep are the things to watch.

A peptide encoded by mitochondrial DNA rather than the nucleus, which is unusual. It activates AMPK and appears to improve how flexibly the body switches between burning carbs and fat. Levels decline with age, and most research is in metabolic and exercise-capacity models rather than weight loss specifically.
A liquid blend formulated to support fat loss alongside diet and training. Ingredient profiles vary, so read the label on the product page. Treat it as an adjunct, not a primary driver.

ERR-alpha is one of the master switches muscle flips on during endurance exercise. Activating it chemically raises fat oxidation and mitochondrial production without the training. Mouse studies showed meaningful fat loss without diet change; there is no human data yet, which is the key caveat.

Combines an exercise mimetic with a mitochondrial uncoupler — one raises fat burning capacity, the other raises baseline energy expenditure. The pairing is aggressive by design. Neither compound has human trial data, so this is firmly experimental territory.

A newer compound in the same series that activates all three ERR receptors rather than just alpha, broadening the metabolic effect. Positioned as a more complete exercise mimetic than SLU-PP-332. Even earlier in development, with correspondingly less data.

Originally developed for Parkinson's, where trial participants lost unexpected amounts of weight. It blocks reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, which suppresses appetite centrally. Capsule form makes dosing simple, but it is a genuine stimulant — expect effects on heart rate, blood pressure and sleep.

Blocks reuptake of all three major monoamines, producing appetite suppression through the brain rather than the gut. It reached phase III trials for obesity with solid weight loss results. It is not a GLP-1 and doesn't behave like one — the side effect profile is stimulant-shaped.

Amylin is released alongside insulin and tells the brain you've eaten enough. This is a long-acting synthetic version, so that fullness signal persists. It is usually run with a GLP-1 rather than alone, and the combination tends to preserve more lean mass than a GLP-1 by itself.

A long-acting amylin analog. Amylin slows stomach emptying and signals satiety through a different pathway than GLP-1, which is why the two stack well. On its own the weight loss is moderate; paired with semaglutide it approaches tirzepatide territory.

Cagrilintide and semaglutide in one vial, hitting amylin and GLP-1 at once. Trial results put it among the strongest weight-loss combinations tested. Because you are stacking two appetite pathways, titration matters more than usual — nausea is the common early complaint.

Semaglutide mimics GLP-1, a gut hormone that slows stomach emptying, blunts appetite and improves insulin response. Weekly dosing, with a slow titration to limit nausea. The best-studied compound in the class, with years of human data behind it.

Tirzepatide hits both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. The GIP arm appears to improve how fat tissue handles nutrients, which is part of why it outperforms semaglutide head-to-head. Weekly dosing with the same titration logic, and gut side effects remain the limiting factor early on.

Tirzepatide and retatrutide combined. The intent is to blend tirzepatide's established tolerability with retatrutide's additional glucagon activity. There are no trials on this specific combination — it's a vendor formulation, not a studied protocol.

Retatrutide adds glucagon receptor activity on top of GLP-1 and GIP. Glucagon raises energy expenditure, so you get appetite suppression plus a metabolic rate effect. It produced the largest weight loss of any incretin in trials to date, and is still investigational — not approved anywhere.

Retatrutide with cagrilintide, adding the amylin pathway to an already triple-acting compound. The rationale is maximum appetite coverage with better lean-mass retention. No trial has tested this combination; it's a stack, not a studied drug.

Semaglutide mimics GLP-1, slowing gastric emptying, reducing appetite and improving insulin sensitivity. Weekly injection with a gradual dose increase to manage nausea. The most thoroughly studied compound in the category.

Tirzepatide activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors, and in direct comparison produces more weight loss than semaglutide. Weekly dosing, titrated upward over months. Nausea, reflux and constipation are the usual early complaints and generally settle.

Retatrutide is a triple agonist — GLP-1 and GIP for appetite, plus glucagon to raise energy expenditure. Trial participants lost more weight than on any previous incretin. It remains investigational, and the glucagon arm means heart rate and liver markers are worth watching.

Retatrutide paired with cagrilintide in a single vial, layering amylin on top of the triple agonist. Aimed at maximum appetite suppression with better lean-mass preservation. No clinical trial has evaluated this specific combination.

Built as an antibody-peptide conjugate, which gives it a much longer half-life than a standard peptide — monthly rather than weekly. Unusually, it blocks GIP while activating GLP-1, the opposite of tirzepatide's approach, and both strategies appear to work. Still in trials.

Activates GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. The glucagon component raises energy expenditure and has shown liver-fat benefits alongside weight loss. Developed primarily in China, where most of the trial data comes from.

A long-acting amylin analog designed to be stable enough for weekly dosing. The appeal is that amylin-driven weight loss appears to spare more lean mass than GLP-1-driven loss. Early-stage compared with the established incretins.

Retatrutide works on three receptors — GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. The glucagon arm raises energy expenditure, which is what separates it from tirzepatide. It has produced the largest weight loss figures of the class in trials and is not yet approved.

Semaglutide mimics the gut hormone GLP-1, slowing digestion and reducing appetite. Weekly dosing, titrated up slowly. It's the most established compound in the category with the longest safety record.

Survodutide activates GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. Beyond weight loss, it has shown strong results for liver fat and fibrosis in trials. Investigational, with the glucagon arm making heart rate worth monitoring.
A dual GLP-1 and glucagon agonist. The glucagon side raises energy expenditure and has produced notable liver-fat improvements in NASH trials. Still in development, not approved.

Tirzepatide hits GIP and GLP-1 together, which outperforms GLP-1 alone in head-to-head trials. Weekly injection with a slow titration schedule. Gut side effects dominate the first few weeks and usually settle as the dose stabilises.

A synthetic peptide researched around hormone signalling and muscle-wasting models. Published literature is very limited — a handful of papers, no human data. Treat anything claimed about it with caution.

A GHRH analog without the DAC attachment, so it clears quickly and produces a short, natural-shaped GH pulse rather than a constant elevation. That pulsatile pattern is closer to normal physiology. Almost always paired with a GHRP, since the two together produce a much larger release than either alone.

The default growth hormone pairing. One tells the pituitary to release, the other amplifies how much comes out, and together they produce a pulse neither achieves alone. Ipamorelin's selectivity means minimal cortisol, prolactin or hunger spike. Usually run before bed to ride the natural overnight pulse.

One of the original growth hormone releasing peptides. It works well but is far less selective than ipamorelin — expect a noticeable cortisol and prolactin bump, and significant hunger. That appetite effect is useful if you're trying to eat more, and a problem if you aren't.

The strongest GHRP by peak GH release, but it desensitises the receptor faster than any other. Run it continuously and the effect fades within weeks. Short, intermittent blocks are the standard approach, and it carries more prolactin and cortisol than ipamorelin.

Pairs the most potent GHRP with a GHRH analog for the largest possible pulse. Powerful, but hexarelin's rapid desensitisation means this isn't something to run continuously. Short cycles with real breaks.

IGF-1 is what growth hormone actually signals through to build tissue. The LR3 modification stops binding proteins from clearing it, so it stays active dramatically longer than natural IGF-1. That potency cuts both ways — it drives growth indiscriminately, which is why blood sugar and tissue-growth concerns come up.

The cleanest of the GH secretagogues. It triggers GH release through the ghrelin receptor but, unlike older GHRPs, barely touches cortisol, prolactin or appetite. That selectivity is the entire reason it's the default choice. Effects are real but gradual — think sleep and recovery over weeks, not a dramatic change.

The most popular GH combination, typically dosed before bed. One drives the release, the other amplifies it, and together they produce a pulse that mimics natural overnight GH output. Most people notice sleep depth first, with recovery and body composition following over a couple of months.

The standard GH secretagogue pairing in a strip that dissolves under the tongue. Convenient if needles are the barrier. Sublingual absorption of peptides this size is less reliable than injection, so expect a weaker effect than the injectable version.

An orally active ghrelin mimetic that raises GH and IGF-1 around the clock rather than in pulses. That constant elevation is both its appeal and its drawback — it works, but it also drives serious hunger, water retention and some insulin resistance. Most people find the appetite effect the deciding factor.
A newer orally active GH secretagogue in the same family as MK-677. Positioned as having a cleaner profile, though there's very little published data to confirm that. Early and largely unvalidated.

The original GHRH fragment, and the mildest option here. Its very short half-life means a brief, natural pulse with no accumulation. Often used as a starting point or in clinical anti-aging settings where a gentle approach is preferred.

A stabilised GHRH analog, and the only GH secretagogue with clinical trial data specifically showing reduced visceral fat — the deep abdominal fat around the organs. It's an approved drug for HIV-associated lipodystrophy. That visceral-fat evidence is what sets it apart from everything else in this group.

Combines the only secretagogue with real visceral-fat data with the cleanest GHRP. Popular for body recomposition where abdominal fat is the target. Expect a slow timeline — this is a months-long protocol, not a quick change.

A fragment of EPO that keeps the tissue-repair signalling but has none of the red-blood-cell effects, so it doesn't thicken the blood. It targets the innate repair receptor, which sits on nerve and immune cells. Most of the human work is in small-fibre neuropathy and sarcoidosis, where it showed real pain improvement.

Derived from a protein found in gastric juice. It promotes new blood vessel growth and gets fibroblasts migrating into damaged tissue, which is why it shows up for tendon, ligament, muscle and gut-lining injuries. Animal data is extensive and consistently positive; human trials are essentially absent, so the enthusiasm runs well ahead of the evidence.

Pairs the repair peptide with KPV's anti-inflammatory action, in capsules aimed at the gut rather than systemic injury. Oral is the sensible route when the gut lining itself is the target, since the peptide acts locally on the way through. For a tendon or muscle injury, injection near the site makes more sense.

The two work on different parts of the same problem — BPC-157 drives local blood vessel and fibroblast activity, TB-500 moves cells into the area from further afield. That complementarity is why they're almost always run together for injuries. Typically dosed for 4-8 weeks around an acute injury rather than continuously.

The arginine salt form, which is far more stable in solution than the acetate version and survives longer once reconstituted. The arginine counterion also contributes some nitric oxide, which may help blood flow to the area. Often sold as PDA or pentadeca arginate.

A short bioregulator peptide targeting cartilage tissue. Research is confined to cell culture — chondrocyte behaviour and the inflammatory profile of aging cartilage. There is no animal or human data, and the osteoarthritis trials you may read about were run on a cartilage extract, not this peptide.

Cartalax layered onto the standard BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV repair stack, aimed at joints specifically. The logic is tissue-repair signalling plus a cartilage-directed bioregulator. It's a vendor formulation rather than a studied combination.

A proprietary repair blend. The exact composition isn't published, which makes it hard to say much with confidence. If you're choosing between this and a named blend, the named one is easier to reason about.

GHK-Cu, TB-500 and BPC-157 together — copper peptide for collagen and skin, plus the two repair peptides. It's the most popular cosmetic-plus-recovery stack, used for skin quality, hair and connective tissue. The copper peptide is what makes it a skin protocol rather than purely an injury one.

GLOW with KPV added, which brings an anti-inflammatory and gut-directed component to the repair trio. Four peptides covering tissue repair, skin and inflammation. Popular as a general recovery protocol rather than for a specific injury.

Three peptides covering different parts of recovery — KPV for inflammation, TB-500 for systemic cell migration, BPC-157 for local tissue repair. Marketed as a comprehensive repair blend. As with all blends, you give up the ability to adjust any single component.

A fatty acid amide your body already makes, which rises naturally in response to tissue damage. It works through PPAR-alpha to calm the immune cells that amplify pain signals, particularly nerve pain. Human trials are reasonably solid for chronic and neuropathic pain, and it's non-opioid with a clean safety record.

Another name for BPC-157, so called because it's fifteen amino acids long. Same compound, same mechanism — angiogenesis and fibroblast migration for tendon, ligament and gut repair. Worth knowing the alias so you don't buy the same thing twice.

The KPV, TB-500 and BPC-157 repair blend in tablet form. Oral dosing suits gut-focused use, where the peptides act locally on the lining. For musculoskeletal injuries, injection remains the route with the supporting data.

A synthetic version of a region of thymosin beta-4, the protein that regulates actin and therefore cell movement. It promotes cell migration and blood vessel growth throughout the body, which makes it the systemic counterpart to BPC-157's local action. Animal data for wound and cardiac repair is good; human data is thin.

The Wolverine stack. BPC-157 works locally at the injury site while TB-500 brings repair cells in from elsewhere, so they address different halves of healing. Run for a defined block around an injury rather than indefinitely.

BPC-157 formulated for topical application directly over the injured area. Appealing for people avoiding injections, though how much peptide of this size actually crosses skin is an open question. Reasonable for superficial tissue, less convincing for a deep tendon.

Copper peptide for collagen and tissue remodelling paired with KPV's anti-inflammatory action. Used where repair and inflammation both need addressing — skin conditions and gut protocols most often. A smaller, more targeted blend than GLOW or KLOW.

The body's primary antioxidant, central to liver detoxification pathways. Oral glutathione is largely destroyed in digestion, which is why injectable and acetylated forms exist. Commonly used for liver support and skin brightening, the latter being a well-documented side effect of the same mechanism.

The last three amino acids of alpha-MSH, which turn out to carry most of its anti-inflammatory activity without the pigmentation effects. It acts on NF-kB, a master inflammatory switch. The strongest case for it is gut inflammation, where it works locally on the lining.

A human antimicrobial peptide, part of your innate immune defence. It kills bacteria directly, breaks up biofilms that shield them from antibiotics, and modulates the immune response. The biofilm activity is the distinctive part — it's used in chronic infection protocols where standard antibiotics stall.

Standard oral glutathione is broken down before absorption. The acetylated form survives digestion and reaches the cell intact, where the acetyl group is removed. That makes it a genuine oral option rather than a waste of money.

A thymus extract rather than a single peptide — the preparation used in the long-running Russian longevity studies that reported reduced mortality in elderly subjects. It's a registered drug in Russia. The mortality trials are frequently cited for synthetic peptides, but it was this extract that was actually tested.

A two-amino-acid thymic peptide, registered as a prescription immunomodulator in Russia for infections with weakened immunity. The approved dose is 100 micrograms — worth knowing, because vials sold here are typically 10mg, a hundred times that. Its anti-aging claim rests on a single rat study.

A thymic peptide that helps T-cells mature and directs the immune response rather than simply ramping it up. It's an approved drug in several countries for hepatitis B and as a vaccine adjuvant, and saw heavy use during COVID. The best-evidenced immune peptide in this list.

A thymus-derived dipeptide from the Russian bioregulator research programme. Cell studies show it loosening tightly-packed DNA in immune cells from elderly donors, reactivating dormant genes. Worth knowing the same study found a near-doubling of a DNA damage marker, which the authors read as activation and toxicologists would read differently.

A signalling peptide found throughout the gut and lungs with broad anti-inflammatory and immune-balancing effects. Most commonly used intranasally in mould illness and chronic inflammatory response protocols. Human evidence outside those niches is limited.

A short bioregulator peptide targeting lung and bronchial tissue. The cell-culture work is some of the better-quantified in the bioregulator family, with markers improving more in older cultures than younger ones. No human data exists.

A bioregulator peptide for heart muscle tissue. The published research is almost entirely inside patent filings rather than peer-reviewed journals, and the one properly published result was in skin-type cells rather than cardiac. Thin evidence even by bioregulator standards.

Sold as a lung bioregulator, but every retrievable experiment on it is about the stomach — an ulcer model with H. pylori, where it performed comparably to an antibiotic. There appear to be two similarly-named organ extracts and the marketing picked the wrong one. If you want it for gut lining, the data supports that; for lungs, it doesn't.

A component of the electron transport chain, the final step of cellular energy production, and a fat-soluble antioxidant. Levels drop with age and are notably depleted by statins. Most useful where mitochondrial energy is the bottleneck — heart function and statin-related muscle complaints.
A bioregulator peptide directed at brain cortex tissue, from the same Russian research programme as the rest of the family. Published data is sparse and largely untranslated. Treat claims cautiously.

A four-amino-acid pineal peptide, and the best-evidenced compound in the bioregulator family. An independent UK lab confirmed in 2025 that it rebuilds telomeres and raises telomerase in human cells — the only finding in this family replicated outside the original Russian group. In mice it extended maximum but not average lifespan. No human telomere study exists.

Alternate spelling of Epitalon, the same four-amino-acid pineal peptide. Used for telomere support and restoring melatonin rhythm. Note the frequently-cited human mortality data belongs to Epithalamin, a pineal extract, not to this synthetic peptide.

A senolytic — it targets senescent cells, the worn-out cells that stop dividing but refuse to die and leak inflammatory signals. It disrupts the protein interaction those cells use to block their own self-destruction. The mouse data is striking; human data doesn't exist, and clearing senescent cells is a blunt intervention.

Shifts haemoglobin's oxygen binding so it releases more oxygen into tissue rather than holding onto it. Studied for endurance, ischemia and tumour oxygenation. It's on the WADA banned list, which tells you the performance effect is considered real.

A liver-directed bioregulator peptide. Cell work shows it has the strongest DNA binding of the bioregulator family and loosens packed chromatin in aged immune cells. The hepatitis patient data circulating for it exists only in a patent filing, not a peer-reviewed journal.

NAD+ in a strip that dissolves under the tongue, which avoids both the injection and the intense flush that IV NAD+ causes. Absorption is lower than injection, so this is a maintenance format rather than a loading one. Convenient enough for daily use.
A blend formulated around mitochondrial function and cellular energy. Composition varies by product, so check the label. Generally combines NAD+ precursors with antioxidant and cofactor support.

The central cofactor for energy production and the fuel sirtuins need to do DNA repair. Levels fall substantially with age, and restoring them is one of the better-supported ideas in longevity. Injected or IV NAD+ causes a distinctive flushing sensation that's dose-rate dependent — go slow.

Pairs NAD+ with carnitine, combining the cellular energy cofactor with the molecule that transports fat into the mitochondria to be burned. The logic is addressing both the fuel delivery and the machinery. Commonly run as part of a metabolic or energy protocol.

NAD+ adjusted to a more physiological pH, which meaningfully reduces the sting and flushing of standard NAD+ injections. Same compound and same effects, better tolerated. Worth the difference if you're dosing regularly.

A three-amino-acid brain bioregulator. The best-designed study — an Alzheimer's mouse model — had its primary endpoint come back negative, though neuron connection density improved modestly. Notably, a rat study found the middle dose outperformed the highest, which is a direct argument against assuming more is better.

GHK-Cu paired with NAD+ — copper peptide for collagen and tissue remodelling alongside the central energy cofactor. Repair signalling plus the cellular energy to act on it. A convenience blend rather than a studied combination.

Targets cardiolipin, a lipid unique to the inner mitochondrial membrane, stabilising the structure where energy production actually happens. That makes it one of the few compounds acting directly on mitochondrial architecture rather than upstream signalling. Human trials exist in heart failure and mitochondrial myopathy with mixed results.

A thymus bioregulator peptide for immune regulation, closely related to Thymogen. Note the naming overlap — Thymogen and Thymagen are often used interchangeably by vendors despite sometimes being listed as separate products. Worth confirming which you're buying.

A bioregulator peptide directed at blood vessel lining. The vascular evidence is a single cell-culture study; its strongest data is actually neurological, from an Alzheimer's mouse model. Sold for one thing, evidenced for another.

Raises dopamine by increasing the enzyme that produces it, and appears to protect dopamine neurons rather than just stimulating them. Rodent work shows an increase in dopamine neuron count in the substantia nigra, the region affected in Parkinson's. Used for motivation and drive, with a neuroprotective rationale behind it.

Two nootropic peptides combined in a sublingual drop format, pairing an anxiolytic with a memory-focused compound. Drops absorb through the mouth lining rather than the gut. Vendor formulations differ, so check what's actually in it.
A nootropic peptide in the Selank family, formulated as a spray. The intent is anxiety reduction without sedation or cognitive dulling. Published research is limited compared with Selank itself.

A newer nootropic peptide structurally related to the Semax family, researched around memory and learning. It's a more recent arrival with correspondingly less published data. Treat it as experimental relative to Semax or Selank.
A specific variant of Adamax. The class numbers denote different formulations or purity classes rather than different compounds. Check the product page for what distinguishes them.
A second Adamax variant. As above, the number refers to the formulation class rather than a separate molecule.
The 1032 Adamax variant in a sublingual spray. Spray format avoids injection and bypasses first-pass liver metabolism. Absorption is less consistent than injection.

A highly bioavailable choline source that crosses the blood-brain barrier, where it becomes acetylcholine — the neurotransmitter underpinning focus, memory and muscle activation. It also produces a short-term growth hormone bump, which is why it shows up in pre-workouts. Some observational data has raised stroke-risk questions at high chronic doses.

A fat-soluble racetam that modulates AMPA receptors with a distinctly calming, anxiolytic character compared with other racetams. Often chosen for creative or verbal work rather than raw focus. Short half-life means multiple daily doses.

An activity enhancer rather than a releasing agent — it amplifies the neurotransmitter release that's already happening rather than forcing a dump. That mechanism means fewer crashes than classic stimulants. It's a successor to selegiline from the same research lineage, and far less studied.

Raises dopamine by upregulating the gene for tyrosine hydroxylase, the enzyme that makes it. Because you're producing more rather than releasing stored dopamine, there's no depletion or crash. Developed as an actoprotector for Soviet athletes, it has an unusual combination of stimulant and anxiolytic effects.

A choline source that also supplies cytidine, which the body converts to uridine for building brain cell membranes. That dual action makes it more structural and longer-acting than alpha-GPC. It has reasonable human trial data in stroke recovery and age-related cognitive decline.

Derived from fisetin, a flavonoid. It inhibits fatty acid synthase, which reduces the lipid peroxidation that damages brain cells during aging. Part of a series of compounds developed specifically as geroneuroprotectors. Preclinical only.

Derived from angiotensin IV, and reported to be orders of magnitude more potent than BDNF at driving new synapse formation. It crosses the blood-brain barrier readily. That potency is the concern as much as the appeal — indiscriminate synaptogenesis is not obviously desirable, and there's no human data.

A Russian antioxidant and membrane stabiliser used widely there for anxiety, stress tolerance and protection against low oxygen. It stabilises neuronal membranes rather than acting on a specific receptor. Most literature is Russian-language and hasn't been independently replicated.

A modafinil analog producing wakefulness and focus without classic stimulant jitter. Reported to be less aggression-promoting than adrafinil, though that comparison rests on anecdote more than data. Like all eugeroics, it works best as an occasional tool rather than a daily one.

A synthetic retro-analog of a cholecystokinin fragment, producing anxiety relief without benzodiazepine-style sedation or dependence. Developed in Russia. The published work is limited and largely untranslated.

Copper peptide and methylene blue suspended in a tallow base for topical use. Combines collagen and skin-repair signalling with methylene blue's mitochondrial and antimicrobial activity. A formulation choice rather than a studied combination.

A lipophilic indole derivative that concentrates in mitochondria, where it scavenges free radicals non-enzymatically. Different mechanism from most antioxidants, which need enzymes to work. Research is focused on neuroprotection.

A curcumin derivative engineered for the bioavailability curcumin itself lacks. It raises BDNF and targets mitochondrial ATP synthase, and is one of the better-performing compounds in Alzheimer's mouse models. It has entered early human trials, which is more than most compounds here.

An alkaloid from corydalis, used in Chinese medicine for centuries. It blocks dopamine D1 and D2 receptors, producing analgesia and sedation. Studied for stimulant craving and chronic pain. Being a dopamine antagonist, it is not a nootropic in the stimulating sense — expect the opposite.

The only magnesium form shown to meaningfully raise magnesium concentration inside the brain, which ordinary magnesium supplements don't achieve. Research centres on synapse density and sleep quality. If you're taking magnesium for sleep or cognition specifically, the form matters.

Semax and Selank in a sublingual strip — one for drive and focus, the other to take the edge off. The pairing is popular precisely because the stimulation and the calm offset each other. Sublingual absorption is less reliable than intranasal or injection.

At low doses it acts as an alternative electron carrier in the mitochondria, bypassing bottlenecks in energy production. At higher doses it becomes an MAO inhibitor, which creates real interaction risk with SSRIs and other serotonergic drugs. Dose matters enormously here — low is the therapeutic window.

A racetam acting on NMDA receptors and calcium channels rather than purely AMPA. Studied specifically for post-stroke apathy and mood rather than raw cognition. Animal toxicity findings at high doses halted some development.
Three nootropic peptides combined in a sublingual spray. Typically a Semax, Selank and supporting compound combination. Check the specific formulation on the product page.
A liquid blend formulated for cognitive support and mental clarity. Ingredients vary by product, so read the label. An adjunct rather than a primary nootropic.
A glutamic acid derivative with anti-amnestic and neuroprotective effects, acting on AMPA receptors. From the Russian nootropic research programme. Limited Western replication.

A dipeptide roughly a thousand times more potent than piracetam by weight, so doses are in the tens of milligrams. It converts to cycloprolylglycine, which raises BDNF and NGF. Among the better-evidenced nootropics with human trial data, and fast-acting enough to feel.

Stimulates the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus and has been shown to increase hippocampal volume. That's an antidepressant mechanism entirely separate from serotonin. It reached phase II trials, where it missed its primary endpoint but improved secondary cognitive measures.

A synthetic analog of ciliary neurotrophic factor, designed to deliver the neurogenic benefits without the side effects of the natural protein. It promotes new brain cell growth in the hippocampus. Preclinical only, with no human data.

An analog of spadin that blocks the TREK-1 potassium channel — a fast-acting antidepressant mechanism that also encourages new neuron growth. The appeal is speed; TREK-1 blockade works in days rather than the weeks SSRIs need. Animal data only.

A GABA-B agonist producing strong anxiety relief and sociability. It genuinely works, which is the problem — tolerance builds within days and withdrawal from regular use is severe and medically significant. If you use it, strictly occasional with multi-day gaps, never daily.

A modified phenylpiracetam where the hydrazide group shifts the profile toward calm rather than stimulation while retaining the memory effects. Useful if standard phenylpiracetam is too activating. Longer-acting than the parent compound.

The original nootropic and the compound that coined the term. It modulates AMPA receptors and improves cell membrane fluidity. Effects are mild and cumulative rather than acute — most people notice little day to day. Doses are large, measured in grams.

A phenylmethylamine derivative with unusually specific evidence: a human trial showed dramatic improvement in verbal retention and word recall, particularly in people with below-average baseline memory. Very long-acting relative to its short half-life, suggesting a downstream mechanism. Limited research beyond that original work.

A synthetic analog of tuftsin, an immune peptide. It reduces anxiety without sedation or cognitive dulling and raises BDNF, so it supports memory at the same time. Typically intranasal. One of the better-tolerated anxiolytics with no dependence profile.

Pairs Selank's daytime anxiolytic action with DSIP's sleep-depth effect in a single spray. The logic is covering both ends of the stress-sleep cycle. A formulation choice rather than a studied combination.

An analog of a fragment of ACTH, stripped of the hormonal activity. It raises BDNF and nerve growth factor, supporting focus, mental stamina and neuroprotection. Used in Russia for stroke recovery. Usually intranasal, and most people notice it within a session rather than over weeks.

The classic nootropic pairing — Semax for drive and focus, Selank to blunt the overstimulation. They're frequently run together because the combination is better balanced than either alone. Both are typically intranasal.

An ampakine active at microgram doses, which makes it one of the most potent compounds in the category by weight. It positively modulates AMPA and NMDA receptors. Potency plus almost no safety data is a meaningful caution — accurate dosing is non-trivial at this scale.

A selective AMPA receptor potentiator engineered to avoid the seizure liability that stalled earlier ampakines. It produces fast antidepressant signals in trials without the dissociative effects of ketamine. Among the more rigorously developed compounds in this category.

A second-generation adenosine A2A receptor antagonist — the same target caffeine hits, but selectively and without caffeine's other actions. A2A blockade raises dopamine signalling, which translates to motivation and motor drive. Developed for Parkinson's rather than as a nootropic.

A nootropic blend in a sublingual strip. Formulation varies — check the product page for what's in it. Convenient format, with the usual caveat that sublingual absorption is less consistent than injection or intranasal.

A mild SARM with partial agonist activity, meaning it only partially activates the androgen receptor. Low suppression relative to the class, and some neuroprotective and cognitive data in animals. Weaker anabolic effect is the trade-off.

A suicidal aromatase inhibitor — it binds the enzyme permanently rather than competitively. Lowering estrogen reduces negative feedback on the pituitary, which can raise LH and testosterone. Driving estrogen too low causes joint pain, poor lipids and low libido, so this is easy to overdo.
A more selective PPAR-delta agonist than Cardarine, with a similar endurance and lipid profile. Less widely used and correspondingly less characterised. Same mechanism, same open questions.

A PPAR-delta agonist that dramatically increases endurance and fat oxidation by shifting muscle toward burning fat. Development was halted when rodents developed cancers across multiple organs at high chronic doses. Those doses were far above typical use, but it's the reason it was abandoned and why WADA bans it.

A second-generation ligandrol analog with a more tissue-selective profile and notable bone density data in animals. The intent was keeping the anabolic effect while reducing suppression. Human data is minimal.

A high-affinity SARM with the best-documented lean mass gains in the class, including human trial data showing meaningful increases over a few weeks. It reliably suppresses natural testosterone, and suppression scales with dose and duration. Recovery timelines vary.

The mildest and most studied SARM, with multiple human trials in muscle wasting. It produces modest lean mass gains with the least suppression of the group, and users frequently report joint relief. The low-risk entry point of the category, though still suppressive.

A potent SARM with a high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio in animal models. Strong suppression is expected, and there are case reports of liver injury at higher doses and longer runs. More aggressive than LGD-4033 in both effect and side effect profile.
An ester-modified RAD-140 designed to stay active longer in the body. Same underlying compound, slower release. Even less human data than RAD-140, which is already limited.

A partial agonist SARM known for a hardening, drying visual effect and some fat loss. Its distinctive side effect is a yellow tint to vision and difficulty adjusting to darkness, caused by binding in the retina — dose-dependent and fully reversible on stopping. That visual effect is why it fell out of favour.

A REV-ERB agonist affecting circadian and mitochondrial gene expression, which is why it's marketed as exercise in a bottle. Oral bioavailability is extremely poor, so most oral products do very little — hence the oil format. The impressive rodent data used injection.

Part SARM, part steroid, and reported to inhibit myostatin by raising follistatin. That myostatin angle is the appeal. It's structurally a steroid despite the SARM label, carries real hepatotoxicity potential, and has essentially no human data.

A tadalafil analog working through the same PDE5 mechanism — it relaxes blood vessels to improve erectile blood flow, and lasts far longer than sildenafil. Because it's an analog rather than the pharmaceutical, consistency between batches varies. The nitrate interaction is the serious one; never combine with nitrates.

The pure trans-isomer of clomiphene, separated out because the other isomer causes most of the mood and visual side effects. It blocks estrogen receptors at the pituitary, which raises LH, FSH and natural testosterone while preserving fertility. That fertility preservation is what makes it the preferred option over TRT for men who want children.

Sits upstream of the whole reproductive hormone cascade — it tells the hypothalamus to release GnRH, which drives LH and FSH. That makes it a more natural lever than injecting hormones further downstream. It also has a distinct central effect on arousal, separate from its hormonal role.
The ten-amino-acid fragment, the form most commonly used. Stimulates the natural LH and FSH cascade and is studied in fertility and hypogonadism contexts. Short half-life means timing matters.

A melanocortin agonist selective for MC1R, so it drives tanning without the libido effect or the nausea that MT-2 causes. It's an approved drug in Europe and the US under the name afamelanotide for a rare light sensitivity disorder. The cleaner option if tanning is the only goal.

A non-selective melanocortin agonist, so it hits MC1R for tanning and MC4R for libido simultaneously. Nausea and facial flushing are common early, and it can darken existing moles — worth a skin check before and after. The non-selectivity is both why it does more than MT-1 and why it's less comfortable.

Melanotan 2 in a sublingual strip, avoiding injections. Expect the same nausea and flushing, since those are systemic rather than route-dependent. Absorption is less predictable than injection, which makes dialling in a dose harder.

A demethylated tadalafil analog using the same PDE5 mechanism for erectile blood flow. As an analog rather than the pharmaceutical, potency varies between batches. The nitrate contraindication applies in full.

Sold as an ovarian or liver bioregulator, but the published research describes kidney cell function. Adding to the confusion, Ovagen is also the name of an unrelated veterinary fertility drug, which makes searching for it difficult. If you want it for ovarian support, the evidence isn't there.

The bonding hormone, involved in social connection, trust and orgasmic response. Typically used intranasally for the social and mood effects, since that route reaches the brain more directly. Effects are context-dependent — it tends to amplify existing social feeling rather than create it.

A prostate-directed bioregulator peptide. The substantial Russian clinical research on prostate peptides was done on Prostatilen, a bovine prostate extract, not on this synthetic peptide. What exists for the peptide itself is cell-culture work and patent filings.

Unlike Viagra and its relatives, this works in the brain on melanocortin receptors rather than on blood flow, so it acts on desire itself rather than mechanics. That makes it effective for both men and women, and it's approved as Vyleesi for low desire in women. Nausea is the common side effect, and it raises blood pressure transiently.

Sold as a testicular bioregulator, but there is essentially no research behind that use. The only primary experiment on the molecule involved binding to wheat proteins, and the citations in its own supporting review don't test it on reproductive tissue. The weakest-evidenced compound in this catalog.

A topical anti-androgen that blocks the androgen receptor at the hair follicle, with minimal systemic absorption compared with finasteride. That local action is the appeal — the hair benefit without the sexual side effects finasteride is known for. It has never been through human trials, and development was abandoned decades ago.

Better known as Argireline. It reduces the neurotransmitter release that drives muscle contraction at the skin surface, softening expression lines. Often marketed as a topical alternative to botox, though the effect is far milder and surface-level. Works on dynamic lines, not static ones.

A copper peptide focused on hair follicle stimulation rather than collagen, often paired with GHK-Cu in hair protocols. It promotes follicle size and the growth phase of the hair cycle. Less studied than GHK-Cu.

A copper-binding tripeptide found naturally in plasma, with levels declining sharply with age. It drives collagen and elastin production, wound remodelling and hair follicle signalling. It's among the best-evidenced cosmetic peptides, with real topical data. Injected forms carry more systemic copper, which is worth considering.
A topical serum formulated for skin tone and brightening. Ingredients vary — check the product page. Topical formulations with a defined active are easier to assess than proprietary blends.

An extension of the Argireline mechanism, reported to be more potent at softening expression lines. Like Argireline, it works on dynamic lines caused by muscle movement rather than sun damage or volume loss. Topical only.

Delta sleep-inducing peptide promotes slow-wave sleep — the deep, physically restorative stage rather than total sleep time. It also modulates the stress axis. Results are notably inconsistent between individuals, with some people reporting a clear effect and others nothing at all.

Liquid melatonin for sleep onset and circadian timing. Melatonin is a timing signal rather than a sedative, so it works best taken a few hours before target sleep time, and low doses often outperform high ones. More is not better here.

A sleep blend in a strip that dissolves under the tongue, bypassing digestion for faster onset. Formulations vary — check what's in it. Sublingual is a sensible route for sleep compounds specifically, since speed matters.
A liquid blend formulated for sleep support. Check the product page for the specific ingredients. Adjunct rather than a primary sleep intervention.

An orexin receptor antagonist — it blocks the signal that keeps you awake rather than sedating you into sleep. That's a fundamentally different and generally cleaner mechanism than benzodiazepines or Z-drugs, with less next-day grogginess and no dependence profile. It has been through phase III trials for insomnia with depression.

Combines direct cellular energy substrates with N-acetyl-L-tyrosine, the precursor your body uses to build dopamine and adrenaline. The tyrosine component is most useful under stress or sleep deprivation, when catecholamine production is the bottleneck. Typically used pre-training or for cognitive demand.

Injectable B12 bypasses the absorption problems that make oral B12 unreliable, particularly in people over 50, vegans, or anyone on metformin or acid blockers. It supports energy metabolism, red cell production and nerve function. Deficiency symptoms are vague, so testing beats guessing.

The three branched-chain amino acids — leucine, isoleucine and valine — with leucine doing most of the muscle-protein signalling. Useful if total protein intake is low or you train fasted. If you're already eating adequate protein, the added benefit is small.

Carnitine shuttles fat into the mitochondria to be burned; arginine is a nitric oxide precursor for blood flow. The pairing targets fat utilisation and delivery at once. Carnitine works best when insulin is present, so timing with a meal matters.

Carnitine for fat transport plus choline for acetylcholine and cell membrane synthesis. The combination covers both the metabolic and the neuromuscular side. Commonly used in fat loss protocols as support rather than a driver.

Carnosine buffers the hydrogen ions that build up during hard training and cause the burn that ends a set; carnitine moves fat into the mitochondria. One targets performance, the other substrate use. Carnosine's effect is cumulative over weeks, not acute.
A liquid blend formulated for energy and focus. Ingredients vary by product — check the label. Typically combines B vitamins, amino acids and nootropic components.
A liquid blend formulated for hair, skin and nails. Usually built around collagen precursors, biotin and supporting cofactors. Check the product page for specifics.

Arginine is the direct precursor to nitric oxide, which dilates blood vessels and improves blood flow. Oral arginine is heavily degraded before it reaches circulation, which is why citrulline often works better; the injectable route avoids that problem.

Carnitine's job is carrying long-chain fatty acids across the mitochondrial membrane so they can be burned. Without enough of it, fat can't reach the furnace. Oral absorption is poor and saturable, which is the main argument for the injectable form.

Citrulline raises blood arginine levels more effectively than arginine itself, because it skips the liver breakdown that destroys most oral arginine. The result is longer-lasting nitric oxide and better blood flow. The counterintuitive one — citrulline beats arginine for raising arginine.

Methylsulfonylmethane is a sulfur donor, and sulfur is structural in connective tissue and cartilage. Used for joint comfort and skin. Reasonable human data for osteoarthritis symptoms at adequate doses.
A liquid blend formulated for pump and blood flow around training. Typically built on nitric oxide precursors. Check the label for the specific actives.
A multi-ingredient liquid amino blend. Composition varies — read the product page. General support rather than a targeted intervention.

Injectable B12 for energy metabolism, red blood cell production and nerve health. The injection bypasses absorption issues common with age, vegan diets, metformin and acid-reducing medication. Deficiency is worth testing for rather than assuming.
A storage case holding ten vials. Peptides degrade with light, heat and movement, so a proper case matters more than it looks. Useful for travel and fridge organisation.
A 3D-printed sliding case for vial storage and transport. Protects against light and knocks. A practical accessory rather than a compound.
A five-vial storage case. Keeps reconstituted vials upright, dark and protected in the fridge.

Dilute acetic acid for peptides that won't dissolve in plain or bacteriostatic water — BPC-157 in particular. The slight acidity breaks the peptide into solution. Only use it where the peptide actually requires it.

A 0.6% acetic acid solution for reconstituting peptides that resist standard water. If a vial stays cloudy or has visible particles after adding bacteriostatic water, this is usually the reason. Check the specific peptide's requirement first.

Acetic acid diluent for peptides needing an acidic solution to go into solution properly. Not interchangeable with bacteriostatic water — using the wrong diluent leaves the peptide partially undissolved and the dose unreliable.

Water with 0.9% benzyl alcohol as a preservative, which is what allows a reconstituted vial to be used repeatedly over about 28 days. That preservative is the entire difference between this and sterile water. Keep it refrigerated once mixed and never freeze a reconstituted vial.

Purified water with no preservative, so a vial reconstituted with it should be used the same day. Suitable for single-use dosing. For anything you'll draw from more than once, bacteriostatic water is the right choice.
A combination storage case sized for mixed vial formats. Keeps a multi-peptide protocol organised and protected in the fridge.
A large-capacity vial storage case for bigger protocols or bulk orders. Light protection and organisation in one.

Phosphate buffered saline holds a stable physiological pH, which matters for peptides that degrade in plain water. Gentler on injection than acidic diluents. Check whether your peptide actually calls for it.

A pH-stable buffered solution used where bacteriostatic water would degrade the peptide. The buffering keeps the solution near physiological pH rather than drifting. Used for more sensitive compounds.

pH-balanced saline for reconstituting peptides sensitive to pH shifts. Also more comfortable to inject than acidic diluents. Not a universal replacement for bacteriostatic water — it has no preservative.

An atomising sprayer attachment for nasal or sublingual dosing, which is the standard route for Semax, Selank and similar peptides. Consistent droplet size matters for consistent dosing. Replace it periodically — they clog.

The diluent used to turn lyophilised powder into an injectable solution. Add it slowly down the inside wall of the vial and swirl gently; never shake, as agitation damages peptide structure. Which diluent to use depends on the peptide.

Preserved reconstitution water at 0.9%, allowing a vial to be used over roughly four weeks once mixed. Refrigerate after reconstituting and don't freeze. The preservative is what buys you the multi-use window.

An empty sterile vial for mixing or splitting a reconstituted peptide across smaller volumes. Useful for blending compounds or dividing an order. Sterile technique matters once you're transferring between vials.
